canonical_fact: The Gray Paper defines a canonical octet-sequence encoding function for protocol values so independent implementations serialize the same state and messages identically.
misconceptions: Different JAM clients may choose any serialization as long as decoded values are equivalent.
title: JAM serialization

canonical_fact: Canonical serialization is part of consensus: equivalent protocol values must encode identically so hashes, signatures and Merkle commitments agree across implementations.
title: Serialization determinism

canonical_fact: JAM defines a state-Merklization function that maps the complete protocol state into a 32-octet cryptographic commitment.

relations.statement: The prior-state root in the header is produced by JAM state Merklization.

title: State Merklization

canonical_fact: JAM specifies a well-balanced binary Merklization construction for protocol data that require balanced-tree commitments.
title: Well-balanced Merklization

canonical_fact: JAM also specifies constant-depth Merkle constructions and page and justification operations for structures needing fixed-depth proofs.
title: Constant-depth Merklization

canonical_fact: JAM uses Blake2b-256 as a 32-octet cryptographic hash function in protocol commitments and identifiers.
title: Blake2b-256

canonical_fact: The Gray Paper defines Keccak-256 as an available standard cryptographic hash function for specified protocol utilities.
title: Keccak-256

canonical_fact: Validator key tuples include Ed25519 public keys used for protocol signatures and identity in specified subsystems such as offender reporting.
title: Ed25519 keys

canonical_fact: Validator key tuples include Bandersnatch keys used by Safrole for seals, VRF outputs and RingVRF constructions.
title: Bandersnatch keys

canonical_fact: Validator key tuples include BLS public keys for protocol cryptographic operations that require BLS signatures.
title: BLS keys

canonical_fact: JAM uses erasure coding to distribute availability data into chunks so original data can be reconstructed from a sufficient subset of validator-held pieces.
misconceptions: Erasure coding removes the need for cryptographic commitments or verification of reconstructed data.

relations.statement: Guarantors reconstruct imported data from enough erasure-coded validator chunks.

title: Erasure coding

canonical_fact: The protocol defines a recovery function inverse to its erasure-coding scheme when enough valid chunks are available.
title: Erasure recovery

canonical_fact: Exported segments are committed in a Merkle structure so later imported segments can be verified with a root, index and proof rather than trusting the supplier.

relations.statement: Segment proofs justify imported data against its Merkle commitment.

title: Segment Merkle commitment

canonical_fact: The Gray Paper treats 32-octet cryptographic values as a common hash-domain type used for code hashes, package hashes, segment roots and other commitments.
title: Hash domain

canonical_fact: JAM's formal serialization, state transition and test vectors are intended to let independent client implementations agree byte-for-byte on protocol behavior.
title: Cross-client conformance
